document.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

questions.question: By what year does NIST expect a review of the AI RMF with formal input from the AI community?

facts.text: The review is expected no later than 2028.

evidence.quote: a review with formal input from the AI community is expected to take place no later than 2028.

questions.question: List all four specific functions in the AI RMF Core.

facts.text: GOVERN.

evidence.quote: These functions – GOVERN , MAP, MEASURE , and MANAGE

facts.text: MAP.

evidence.quote: These functions – GOVERN , MAP, MEASURE , and MANAGE

facts.text: MEASURE.

evidence.quote: These functions – GOVERN , MAP, MEASURE , and MANAGE

facts.text: MANAGE.

evidence.quote: These functions – GOVERN , MAP, MEASURE , and MANAGE

questions.question: In the AI RMF definition, what two components make up the composite measure called risk?

facts.text: The probability of an event occurring.

evidence.quote: risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.

facts.text: The magnitude or degree of that event's consequences.

evidence.quote: risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.

questions.question: How do the AI RMF definitions of reliability and accuracy differ? Include the conditions and time requirement for reliability and the reference used for accuracy.

facts.text: Reliability is performing as required without failure for a given time interval under given conditions.

evidence.quote: ability of an item to perform as required, without failure, for a given time interval, under given conditions

facts.text: Accuracy is closeness of observations, computations, or estimates to true values or values accepted as true.

evidence.quote: closeness of results of observations, computations, or estimates to the true values or the values accepted as being true.

questions.question: Which two data-minimizing methods for certain model outputs does the Privacy-Enhanced section name, and what accuracy tradeoff can privacy-enhancing techniques create under data sparsity?

facts.text: De-identification is a named data-minimizing method.

evidence.quote: data minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs

facts.text: Aggregation is a named data-minimizing method.

evidence.quote: data minimizing methods such as de-identification and aggregation for certain model outputs

facts.text: Under conditions such as data sparsity, privacy-enhancing techniques can reduce accuracy, affecting decisions about fairness and other values.

evidence.quote: Under certain conditions such as data sparsity, privacy- enhancing techniques can result in a loss in accuracy, affecting decisions about fairness and other values in certain domains.

questions.question: What are the three major categories of AI bias identified by NIST, and can they occur without discriminatory intent?

facts.text: Systemic bias.

evidence.quote: three major categories of AI bias to be considered and managed: systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive.

facts.text: Computational and statistical bias.

evidence.quote: three major categories of AI bias to be considered and managed: systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive.

facts.text: Human-cognitive bias.

evidence.quote: three major categories of AI bias to be considered and managed: systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive.

facts.text: Each category can occur without prejudice, partiality, or discriminatory intent.

evidence.quote: Each of these can occur in the absence of prejudice, partiality, or discriminatory intent.

questions.question: How does the Framework distinguish explainability from interpretability?

facts.text: Explainability represents the mechanisms underlying AI system operation: how a decision was made.

evidence.quote: Explainability refers to a representation of the mechanisms underlying AI systems’ oper- ation
Ex- plainability can answer the question of “how” a decision was made in the system.

facts.text: Interpretability concerns the meaning of outputs in their functional context: why a decision was made and its meaning or context for the user.

evidence.quote: interpretability refers to the meaning of AI systems’ output in the context of their designed functional purposes.
Inter- pretability can answer the question of “why” a decision was made by the system and its meaning or context to the user.

questions.question: Which GOVERN subcategory addresses inventorying AI systems, and how should those mechanisms be resourced?

facts.text: GOVERN 1.6 addresses mechanisms to inventory AI systems.

evidence.quote: GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems

facts.text: The mechanisms should be resourced according to organizational risk priorities.

evidence.quote: GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.

questions.question: What median annual salary in US dollars does the Framework report for an AI risk manager?
questions.absence_reason: The document describes AI actor roles and risk management responsibilities but contains no salary survey or median salary for an AI risk manager.

questions.question: How many training tokens does the AI RMF recommend for a seven-billion-parameter language model?
questions.absence_reason: The document discusses model training risks and large language models, but gives no model-size-specific training token budget.

questions.question: What percentage score is required to pass the NIST AI RMF professional certification exam described in this document?
questions.absence_reason: The document does not describe a NIST AI RMF professional certification exam or a passing percentage; references to training and certifications do not specify such an exam.

questions.question: What average price per thousand cloud inference requests does the Framework report?
questions.absence_reason: The document mentions cloud services and computational costs but provides no inference pricing or average price per thousand requests.

questions.question: What does comparing an AI RMF Current Profile with a Target Profile reveal, and what can be developed to address the result?

facts.text: The comparison reveals gaps to address to meet AI risk management objectives.

evidence.quote: Comparing Current and Target Profiles likely reveals gaps to be addressed to meet AI risk management objectives.

facts.text: Action plans can be developed to address the gaps and fulfill category or subcategory outcomes.

evidence.quote: Action plans can be developed to address these gaps to fulfill outcomes in a given category or subcategory.

questions.question: Does the AI RMF prescribe risk tolerance, and what should organizations do when established tolerance guidelines do not exist?

facts.text: The AI RMF does not prescribe risk tolerance.

evidence.quote: While the AI RMF can be used to prioritize risk, it does not prescribe risk tolerance.

facts.text: Organizations should define reasonable risk tolerance when established guidelines do not exist.

evidence.quote: Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should define reasonable risk tolerance.

questions.question: When in the AI lifecycle are TEVV tasks performed, and ideally how should verification and validation actors relate to test and evaluation actors?

facts.text: TEVV tasks are performed throughout the AI lifecycle.

evidence.quote: Test, Evaluation, Verification, and Validation (TEVV) tasks are performed throughout the AI lifecycle.

facts.text: Ideally, actors performing verification and validation are distinct from those performing test and evaluation.

evidence.quote: Ideally, AI actors carrying out verification
and validation tasks are distinct from those who perform test and evaluation actions.

questions.question: Which three types of drift can cause AI systems to need more frequent maintenance and corrective-maintenance triggers?

facts.text: Data drift.

evidence.quote: maintenance due to data, model, or concept drift.

facts.text: Model drift.

evidence.quote: maintenance due to data, model, or concept drift.

facts.text: Concept drift.

evidence.quote: maintenance due to data, model, or concept drift.

questions.question: What should happen to development and deployment when an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk levels, and until when?

facts.text: Development and deployment should cease in a safe manner.

evidence.quote: development and deployment should cease in a safe manner until risks can be sufficiently managed.

facts.text: They should remain stopped until the risks can be sufficiently managed.

evidence.quote: development and deployment should cease in a safe manner until risks can be sufficiently managed.

questions.question: How does the Framework distinguish security from resilience in their relationship to adverse events and attacks?

facts.text: Resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event.

evidence.quote: While resilience is the abil- ity to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event

facts.text: Security includes resilience and protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks.

evidence.quote: security includes re- silience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover from attacks.

questions.question: How many penetration tests per year does the Framework require every AI system to undergo?
questions.absence_reason: The document discusses testing and security risk management but sets no universal annual number of penetration tests.

questions.question: What federal grant amount in dollars does an organization receive for adopting AI RMF 1.0?
questions.absence_reason: The document presents voluntary framework adoption and organizational resource considerations but specifies no adoption grant program or dollar amount.
